Relevant text: interval 'The default is 30 seconds' for instance targets; timeout 5 seconds; HealthyThresholdCount 'The default is 5'; UnhealthyThresholdCount 'The default is 2'; Matcher 'The default value is 200'; reason code Target.ResponseCodeMismatch, 'Health checks failed with these codes: [code]'; 'If a target group contains only unhealthy registered targets, the load balancer routes requests to all those targets, regardless of their health status ... the load balancer fails open.'

sources.cite: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling User Guide: Health checks for instances in an Auto Scaling group
sources.note: Read through a summarizing fetch on 2026-11-16. Relevant text: 'When Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling determines that an InService instance is unhealthy, it replaces it with a new instance to maintain the desired capacity of the group'; Elastic Load Balancing is one of the sources that can report an instance unhealthy; the checks begin after a health check grace period. The default grace period was not stated on the page, so the scenario gives the group's setting.

brief.situation: You are the CloudOps engineer for Ferncastle Outdoor, a fictional retailer. Release v3.4 went out at 08:20 by an instance refresh. Since then 5xx errors are at 12% and instances keep being replaced. The spring campaign email goes to 400,000 customers at 10:00 and will triple traffic.
handover: The site is an Application Load Balancer in front of web-asg (6 instances, ELB health checks, 300 s grace period).
The campaign landing pages ship in v3.4.
howItWorks: The board shows the load balancer, the Auto Scaling group, the application and the business, and updates as you work.
Each task takes your time: start it, then let the work finish, which moves the clock by the minutes it takes. The group and the campaign keep to the same clock.
When you close the incident, you write the record and explain your reasoning.

source.note: The campaign email goes out at 10:00, an hour after the 09:00 start.

How many minutes each command or task takes, and when the fictional problem spreads, are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values. With ELB health checks, every ten minutes two more instances are terminated and replaced; replacements fail the same check after the grace period.

writeup.question: For the record: what the health check was telling you, what you changed, and why that was the right layer.

parts.label: Evidence
parts.criteria: Uses the target health reason (ResponseCodeMismatch 302) and the activity history to show the instances were healthy and the check was wrong.
parts.modelAnswer: Target health showed Target.ResponseCodeMismatch with 302 on every target, the activity history showed the group terminating instances for ELB health check failures, and a request from an instance showed /health redirecting to /login while /healthz returned 200.

parts.label: Fix
parts.criteria: Points the check at an unauthenticated health endpoint with 200 as the only success code, rather than accepting redirects or switching off replacement.
parts.modelAnswer: I changed the path to /healthz with matcher 200; widening the matcher would pass a dead app, and suspending ReplaceUnhealthy only hides the failure while the load balancer fails open.

parts.label: Stability
parts.criteria: Stops the churn before the campaign, leaves automatic replacement working, and adds an alarm on unhealthy hosts.
parts.modelAnswer: Targets were healthy within about three minutes, before 10:00; replacement stayed on, and an UnHealthyHostCount alarm now pages on-call.

scoring.modelReasoning: Every target is unhealthy with Target.ResponseCodeMismatch 302, and the group, which uses ELB health checks, keeps terminating and replacing instances; with all targets unhealthy the load balancer fails open, so the errors come from instances being terminated mid-request. A request from an instance shows /health now redirects to /login while the release added /healthz. Change the health check path to /healthz with 200 as the only success code; the targets turn healthy after five passing checks (about 150 seconds), well before the 10:00 campaign. Do not widen the matcher (it would pass a dead app) or leave ReplaceUnhealthy suspended (real failures would stay in service); add an UnHealthyHostCount alarm and make the health endpoint part of release tests.
